questions.explanation: The Sine Rule relates each side to the sine of its opposite angle: $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}$.

questions.stem: When should you use the Sine Rule rather than the Cosine Rule?

options.text: When you know all three sides
When you know two sides and the included angle
When you know two angles and a side, or two sides and a non-included angle

questions.explanation: The Sine Rule is used when you have a matching pair (angle and its opposite side) plus one other piece of information — typically AAS, ASA, or SSA.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $A = 40°$, $B = 60°$, and $a = 10$ cm. Find $b$ to $1$ decimal place.
In triangle $PQR$, $p = 12$ cm, $q = 8$ cm, and $P = 50°$. Find angle $Q$ to $1$ decimal place.
Why can the Sine Rule sometimes give two possible answers for an angle (the ambiguous case)?

options.text: Because $\sin \theta = \sin(180° - \theta)$, so there may be two valid angles
Because the triangle might not exist
Because the calculator gives a rounding error

questions.explanation: Since $\sin \theta = \sin(180° - \theta)$, both $\theta$ and $180° - \theta$ are possible solutions. You must check which one gives a valid triangle.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $A = 35°$, $C = 80°$, and $c = 15$ cm. Find $a$ to $1$ decimal place.
In triangle $ABC$, $B = 65°$ and $C = 48°$. What is angle $A$?
